idiom_name: Iterable<T>.filter / Sequence<T>.filter with (T) -> Boolean function types (inline lambdas)
implementation_notes: The standard library takes the criterion as a value: Iterable<T>.filter(predicate: (T) -> Boolean): List<T> is eager, and Sequence<T>.filter returns another sequence whose operation is documented as intermediate and stateless, so the lazy form chains without building lists. The classic filterer object collapses into the container's own method - fun filtered(keep: (Threat) -> Boolean) = ThreatAwareSystem(systemId, threats.filter(keep)) - because function types are the first-class criteria and inline extension functions avoid allocating a Function object per call. filterNot, filterIndexed, filterIsInstance, filterNotNull and partition cover the common criterion shapes, and criteria compose with && or by wrapping. Kotlin's function types are already contravariant in their parameter (Function1<in P, out R>) and read-only collections are declaration-site covariant, so the Java-style covariant Filterer indirection is unnecessary; keep an explicit filterer type only for Java interop or when criteria must be stored as data.
pitfalls: Iterable and Sequence are easy to confuse: every Iterable.filter materialises a list, while a Sequence re-runs the whole chain on each terminal operation and, if it is backed by a single-shot iterator, can be consumed only once.

Storing a criterion as a property or parameter of non-inline type allocates a Function object and blocks inlining; keeping criteria in inline lambdas or data classes of parameters preserves the zero-cost property.

Java interop: a Kotlin lambda passed where java.util.function.Predicate is expected works via SAM conversion, but a Predicate received from Java does not compose with Kotlin's && and must be adapted before it can be combined.
